why: Survey sampled only dog owners, not all city residents — sampling method is not random from the target population. Student must identify the bias (CL.0131) and match the flaw to the claim (CL.0054).
Random sample drawn from people who liked the book; asks which inference can be drawn. Student must match the conclusion to the sampled population (book-likers, not all moviegoers or readers).

Random sample of 200 residents, 87% satisfied. Asks whether statements about exact population value or future sample results MUST be true — neither is guaranteed. Student recognizes sample statistic is an estimate, not a certainty.
Random sample of history professors from CA State Universities; asks for the largest population to which results generalize. Student matches conclusion scope to the sampled population.

Random sample of 1,000 adults, 78% satisfied. Three statements assert exact replication — none must be true. Student recognizes sample variability: a statistic estimates but does not guarantee the parameter or future samples.

Scientist randomly selected baobab trees of a certain age from one habitat; asks the largest group to which results apply. Student matches the conclusion to the sampled population (that age group in that habitat).

Tabitha surveyed families at a playground — a convenience sample, not random from all community households. Student identifies the sampling method as flawed because playground families are not representative.

Viewers self-selected to respond to an online poll on a cable news show — voluntary response bias, not a random sample. Student identifies that respondents were not randomly selected from the US population.

Random sample of 35 students from one middle school; asks the largest group to which results generalize. Student matches the scope to all students at that school (the population the sample was drawn from).
Organizer selected teams at random from all trivia teams in the tournament; asks the largest population. Student matches the conclusion to the sampled population (all teams in the tournament).
Random sample of 40 fourth-graders from a certain school; asks the largest population. Student matches scope to the sampled population — all fourth-grade students at that school.
